purpose: Record what each shell does with constructs outside their common portable subset, so a script's choice of interpreter is measured rather than assumed.
note: Program names are not semantic versions. In particular, observed dash builds exist both without and with ANSI-C quote support. Each installed program must match exactly one complete profile across every case; alternatives are never accepted case by case. `cargo xtask posix-divergence` also runs the same exact script bytes through `/bin/sh` and compares that result with the selected profiles. Most differences are silent, which is why every profile and every case is recorded explicitly.

cases.name: ansi-c-quoting-in-a-case-pattern
cases.script:
case "a
b" in *$'\n'*) echo MATCHED ;; *) echo NO_MATCH ;; esac
cases.note: A newline check written with `$'\n'` silently fails under a shell without ANSI-C quoting because the pattern remains literal text.

cases.name: ansi-c-quoting-expansion
cases.note: Without ANSI-C quoting the word is left as written; with it the argument is one tab byte.

cases.name: double-bracket-test
cases.note: `[[` is a keyword rather than a portable builtin; a shell without it attempts a command and reaches the opposite branch.

cases.name: brace-expansion
cases.note: Without brace expansion the word is one literal argument rather than two.

cases.name: substring-expansion
cases.note: A shell without substring expansion reports a syntax error instead of running the command.

cases.name: local-in-a-function
cases.note: `local` is outside the common portable subset, although every recorded profile implements it.

cases.name: echo-suppress-newline
cases.note: The case records whether `-n` is an option or a word to print.

cases.name: echo-backslash-in-a-variable
cases.note: The case records whether the echo builtin rescans its argument for escapes.

cases.name: ansi-c-newline-and-tab
cases.note: ANSI-C quoting decides the word's newline and tab bytes before `printf` reads it.

cases.name: ansi-c-escaped-backslash
cases.note: The script contains two backslashes; the harness supplies those exact bytes on standard input so a native argv layer cannot consume one.

cases.name: ansi-c-unknown-escape
cases.note: Profiles differ on both recognizing ANSI-C quotes and retaining an unknown escape's backslash.

cases.name: ansi-c-single-quote
cases.note: Recognizing ANSI-C quotes makes the escaped single quote data; without them it leaves an unterminated quote.
